task_title: Apply prompt engineering techniques (zero-shot, few-shot, chain-of-thought)
title: Zero-shot misroutes 3 of 8 claims: show the edges, reason, then label
stem: Harbour Mutual's triage classifier routes motor claims into four routes using a zero-shot prompt with a one-line definition of each route. On the eval set it handles plain claims well but misroutes the same boundary cases on every run: quotes just over US$5,000 before the excess is deducted, a third-party-only policyholder whose victim is claiming, and own-damage write-offs on third-party policies. Which change most directly fixes these errors?

options.A: Switch the classifier to Claude Opus 5.5, which knows enough about motor insurance to settle these cases without examples.
options.B: Ask for a confidence score with every label, and send each claim scored below 0.8 to a human adjuster for routing.
options.C: Add "Think very carefully about edge cases and double-check every label" to the end of the existing system prompt.
options.D: Add worked examples of exactly these boundary cases to the prompt, each with brief reasoning written before its label.

why: The errors are systematic: the one-line definitions leave Harbour's boundary conventions open (the authority applies to the payout after the excess; third-party cover pays the other party's damage), and zero-shot the model guesses the same way every time. Few-shot examples placed on those boundaries show how Harbour applies its rules, and reasoning written before the label makes the model work each case through before it commits.

wrong.A: A bigger model costs more per claim and still has to guess Harbour's own conventions, which only examples or rules supply.
wrong.B: The wrong labels are systematic and given confidently, so a self-reported score will not catch them, and it adds adjuster work.
wrong.C: A plea for care names no convention, so the model has nothing new to apply on the boundary cases.

fix: Few-shot examples on the boundary cases, each with reasoning before the label.
see: Zero-shot gets the plain claims right and misroutes CLM-7790, 7815 and 7821; with six worked examples and reasoning first, all eight route correctly.
explain: The eight claims carry an adjusters' answer key. Zero-shot, with thinking off as a high-volume classifier would run, the plain claims route correctly and the boundaries do not: a US$5,600 quote whose payout after the US$750 excess is US$4,850 goes to an adjuster, so does the claim for the van Daniel reversed into, and his own write-off goes to an adjuster instead of being declined. Six worked examples on those boundaries, each with a line of reasoning, and a schema that asks for reasoning before the label, route all eight correctly. The cost is a longer prompt and more output tokens per claim.
exam_tip: Few-shot examples fix systematic errors on the cases a definition leaves open; reasoning before the answer helps on cases that need several steps. Confidence scores and 'be careful' instructions do not teach the model anything new.
headline: Show the boundary cases. Reason, then label.

concepts.b: Instructions and definitions only, no examples. It works when the task is clear from the definitions; it fails systematically where they leave a boundary open.
A few input-output pairs in the prompt show the format and how your organisation applies its rules. Choose them to cover the boundaries, and vary them.
Asking for reasoning before the answer lets the model work through the steps first. In structured outputs, put the reasoning field before the label field.
If the same cases fail on every run, the prompt is missing information. More confidence or a bigger model rarely fixes that; better examples usually do.
